value.overview: The Hudsonian Whimbrel is a large New World shorebird that breeds in northern Canada and Alaska and migrates through the Americas to wintering areas from Mexico and the Caribbean south to South America. It is recognizable by its long, downcurved bill, brown streaked plumage, and distinctive rapid, rippling call. The species uses tundra during the breeding season and coastal mudflats, beaches, mangroves, salt marshes, and estuaries during migration and winter.
value.classification: The Hudsonian Whimbrel belongs to the sandpiper family Scolopacidae and the curlew genus Numenius. It was formerly treated as the New World subspecies Numenius phaeopus hudsonicus, but modern taxonomic checklists recognize it as a separate species from the Eurasian Whimbrel.
value.identification: This tall, long-legged shorebird has a compact brown body, a small rounded head, and a very long bill that curves downward. The crown and face are strongly streaked, with a pale stripe over the eye and dark stripes through the eye. The back is mottled brown, while the underparts are lighter and heavily streaked on the neck and breast. In flight, the rump and back appear dark rather than showing the broad white rump of the Eurasian Whimbrel. It is larger and more heavily built than most similarly sized sandpipers.
value.rangeHabitat: Hudsonian Whimbrels breed across Arctic and subarctic tundra in Alaska and Canada, including areas around Hudson Bay. They migrate through North, Central, and South America and winter mainly along tropical and subtropical coasts. In Costa Rica, they are regular migrant and winter visitors, occurring chiefly on both the Pacific and Caribbean coasts. They favor exposed intertidal mudflats, sandy beaches, estuaries, salt marshes, mangrove edges, coastal lagoons, and other open wetland shores, and are less common inland.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Hudsonian Whimbrels pass through Costa Rica during northbound and southbound migration, and some remain there during the nonbreeding season. Numbers may vary by coastal site and tidal conditions, with passage and wintering birds concentrated in productive estuaries and mudflats.
value.breeding: Breeding begins after arrival on the Arctic tundra. Pairs usually nest on the ground in open wet lowlands or somewhat drier upland heath with grasses, sedges, mosses, lichens, and low shrubs. The nest is a shallow depression lined with plant material. Both adults defend the nesting territory, incubate the eggs, and care for the chicks. Young birds leave the nest soon after hatching and forage under parental supervision. Costa Rica is outside the breeding range.
value.dietFeeding: Hudsonian Whimbrels feed mainly on crabs and other marine invertebrates, including shrimp, worms, mollusks, and insects. They probe mud and wet sand with the sensitive tip of the bill and pull prey from burrows or surface sediments. Fiddler crabs can be especially important in tropical coastal habitats. They may also take small fish, amphibians, berries, and other foods when available, particularly at inland stopover sites or on the breeding grounds.
value.behavior: These whimbrels usually forage singly or in loose groups, walking steadily across mudflats and beaches while probing the substrate. They often feed around falling or low tides and gather in flocks at high-tide roosts, sometimes with other shorebirds. Migrating birds are powerful fliers and may cross large ocean areas. Their loud, bubbling, rippling calls are often heard before the birds are seen. They can become restless and vocal when disturbed by people, dogs, vehicles, or predators.

conservation.populationTrend: The population trend is concerning. Monitoring conducted before the taxonomic split indicated a major decline in the broader Whimbrel population, although the strength of the trend may differ among breeding and migratory populations.
conservation.threats: Important threats include loss and degradation of coastal wetlands, disturbance at feeding and high-tide roosting sites, climate-driven changes to tundra and coastal habitats, pollution, hunting in parts of the migratory range, and reduced food availability. Sea-level rise, stronger storms, and changes in crab and other invertebrate populations may affect important stopover and wintering areas, including coastal sites in Costa Rica.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore mangroves, estuaries, mudflats, salt marshes, and coastal lagoons used by shorebirds. In Costa Rica, avoid disturbing feeding and roosting flocks, keep dogs under control near shorebird habitat, and support protected coastal wetlands and responsible ecotourism. Reducing plastic and other pollution, reporting observations through reputable bird-monitoring programs, and supporting international shorebird conservation can also improve knowledge and protection across the migration route.
